title: People who cannot manage their thirst. Part 4
scripture_text: ‘’The Pharisees heard the crowd whispering such things about him. Then the Chief Priests and the Pharisees sent temple guards to arrest him. Jesus said “I am with you for only a short time and then I am going to the one who sent me. You will look for me, but you will not find me; and where I am, you cannot come.” The Jews said to one another, “Where does this man intend to go that we cannot find him? Will he go where our people live scattered among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks? What did he mean when he said, ‘You will look for me, but you will not find me,’ and ‘Where I am, you cannot come’?”
devotional:
On the last and greatest day of the festival, Jesus stood and said in a loud voice, “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from within them.” By this he meant the Spirit whom those who believed in him were later to receive. Up to that time the Spirit had not been given, since Jesus had not yet been glorified. On hearing his words, some of the people said, “Surely this man is the Prophet.” Others said, “He is the Messiah.” Still others asked, “How can the Messiah come from Galilee? Does not Scripture say that the Messiah will come from David’s descendants and from Bethlehem the town where David lived?” Thus the people were divided because of Jesus. Some wanted to seize him, but no one laid a hand on him. Finally the temple guards went back to the chief priests and the Pharisees, who asked them, “Why didn’t you bring him in?” “No one ever spoke the way this man does,” the guards replied. “You mean he has deceived you also?” the Pharisees retorted.“Have any of the rulers or the Pharisees believed in him? No! But this mob that knows nothing of the law—there is a curse on them.”

Now that we have seen the context of Jesus’ words, we are better able to understand what he is saying, and more able to apply it to our lives.

As people, our lives are producing some kind of ‘water’ i.e. ‘life’ – we are characterized either by ‘living water’ or ‘dead water’. "Living water" is a phrase used for flowing or fresh water, e.g. "running water" in English. Flowing water is usually drinkable water which is vital for us to live.

The people who were opposing Jesus in this context, represented those in need of living water, people who were unable to manage their thirst. The things that came out of their hearts like hatred and murder indicated that they that they were full of ‘dead water’ and in need of new life, of ‘living water.’

The quality of our lives depends upon the work of the Holy Spirit in us. John informs us ‘By this he meant the Spirit whom those who believe in him would later receive.’ (v39). The way Jesus describes the work of the Holy Spirit in the life of a believer is wonderful. We are all in need of the ongoing refreshing work of the Spirit in our lives. The work of the Spirit within us is to continually refresh us so we can endure the pressures of life in a sinful world. We tend to think of the Holy Spirit as a doctrine to be studied, but for the first believers, the Spirit was understood as someone who empowered and refreshed their lives.

Our ability to receive and be matured by the Holy Spirit depends on what kind of relationship we have with Jesus. As we open up our lives to the Lord Jesus, we are more able to receive and experience the ministry of the Holy Spirit. We need to relate to Jesus as thirsty people. It is people who recognise their thirst for real life that are most able to relate to Jesus.

The main focus of the work of the Spirit in our lives is internally, dealing with our characters and emotions. What flows out of our lives is a reflection of the content of our hearts. Real and lasting change cannot take place in our hearts unless the river from within becomes the thing that distinguishes us. When our hearts are full of emotions and attitudes that are contrary to the fruit of the Spirit, then we will not experience the satisfaction we long for.

There is a sense that what we have received from God is not meant to stay within us, but is to flow out of us. "Water" that stays still becomes stagnant. Could the same thing happen to our faith if it is not shared with others?

Verse 39 says ‘Up to this time the spirit had not been given, since Jesus had not been glorified.’ The oldest and best manuscripts do not contain the word "given." They literally say, "The [Holy] Spirit was not yet, because Jesus had not been glorified" NRSV: reads "For as yet there was no Spirit, because Jesus was not yet glorified". For John the meaning of Jesus being glorified is the crucifixion. John does not mean that the Holy Spirit did not exist until the Cross. After all John's gospel speaks in chapter 1 of the Holy Spirit descending and remaining on Jesus. What he means is that the Holy Spirit won’t be fully experienced by people and realised in their lives until after the crucifixion. It can be summed up by saying that Pentecost was not really possible until the events of Calvary had taken place. Thirsty people need to come to the cross – the thirst we all carry can only be quenched by a meaningful encounter with God and his love for us through the death of his Son.

More confusion about Jesus’ identity.

Although the crowds heard Jesus speak with the same hope, boldness and love as the temple guards, it did not diminish any confusion they had. The Jews expected a fresh outpouring of the Holy Spirit when the Messiah came. They were keenly aware that the Holy Spirit had been the source of prophecy in the Old Testament and no prophets had arisen since Malachi about 400 B.C. They yearned for a fresh outpouring of the Spirit that would be demonstrated by the renewal of prophecy. When Jesus proclaimed the Spirit as living water coming again in abundance from himself, one logical conclusion would be, that Jesus was declaring himself to be the Messiah.

On the other hand some in the crowd could not accept that Jesus was the Messiah because they assumed he was from Galilee, not from Bethlehem. This was the second time they used this argument during the week of the feast. They held onto old conclusions, refusing to make enquires or learn new things.

Speaking clearly and with authority does not guarantee that all people will hear and accept what we have to say. Doing things right, and with right motives will not ensure success, but it will mean that we can stand before God with a clear conscience.

The response of the Jewish leaders

The temple guards return empty-handed not because they had been rendered powerless by Jesus (compare with their later experience in John 18:3-6), nor because they feared the crowds, for some among the crowds also wanted to seize him (contrast later, Mt 26:5 par. Mk 14:2 par. Lk 22:2, 6). Rather, they are struck by the uniqueness of Jesus' message (7:46). This probably accounts for the fact that they were gone for four days (cf. 7:14, 32, 37) instead of an hour or so, as the authorities might have expected! It is right that they should be struck by Jesus' teaching. Here, the eternal Word was speaking about himself, about God and about the salvation he had brought in fulfilment of the promises made through the prophets. Jesus' very way of speaking was unique, as befit his unique message: I.V.P

Notice how the leaders react to the returning guards. They don’t ask the guards what makes Jesus so compelling. Nor do they debate the merits of his claims and they certainly don’t suggest that they would like to hear him for themselves. Instead they do a number of things:

A. They ridicule the guards (v.47) "You mean He has deceived you too?" The message is clear, they were asking how the guards could be so stupid and gullible. It's a common form of argument, attack your opponent, then perhaps you won't have to deal with the issue.

B. They try to coerce through peer pressure. (v. 48) "Have any of the rulers or the Pharisees believed in Him?" The message again is clear. If the leaders don't believe in Jesus, then anyone who has any sense won't believe in him either.

C. They belittle and judge the opposition. (v. 49) "No, but this mob that knows nothing of the law, there is a curse on them." Here they insult all who believe in Jesus, referring to them as a gang, an unruly mob, the radicals of their day. The implication is clear - "If you don't want to be known as a rebel…renounce Him."

D. They would not listen to wise advice. We read that Nicodemus who had gone to Jesus earlier and who was one of their number asked, “Does our law condemn anyone without hearing him to find out the facts?”’ John 7:50 and yet they rejected what he had to say.

E. They told outright lies. When they responded to Nicodemus by saying that a prophet does not come out of Galilee, John 7:52, that was not true, for many believed Jonah was from there.

Often we are like these religious leaders, we have come to some conclusions, and we are determined to avoid facts and truth at all costs, so we do mental gymnastics, twist words, ignore realities, in our desperation to avoid Jesus, and in doing so we remain in our thirst, expressing it in perverted and harmful ways.

As we consider the courage of Jesus in this passage and hear his gracious invitation to all who are thirsty, let us not make the same mistakes as the Pharisees. Let the thirst for life drive us to him, who is the only true source of living water and life everlasting.
prayer: Father may living water flow from my life.
